parts.title: Measuring Many Hormone-Disrupting Chemicals in Newborn Babies' First Poop: The First Evidence of "Forever Chemicals" (PFASs) in Meconium
parts.abstract:
Many people are worried that pregnant women and their babies are exposed to endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs). These are chemicals that can interfere with the body's hormones, the chemical messengers that control growth, development and many other processes. We need good ways to measure how much of these chemicals people are exposed to during pregnancy. Such measurements can help us take steps to prevent harm and predict possible health problems.

Meconium, the first poop a newborn baby passes, has proven to be a valuable material for this job. Collecting it does not hurt the baby. It also builds up the baby's exposure to foreign chemicals during the last two three-month periods of pregnancy, so it shows the total exposure over that time.

Our goal was to develop a new method for finding four groups of EDCs in meconium: perfluoroalkyl substances (PFASs), bisphenols, parabens and benzophenones. PFASs are often called "forever chemicals" because they break down extremely slowly. All four groups are widely used to make many everyday products and personal care products, including cosmetics. We measured ten PFASs, two bisphenols, four parabens and four benzophenones.

To prepare the samples, we combined three techniques. First, we passed the liquid through small tubes called Captiva Enhanced Matrix Removal (EMR) lipid cartridges, which trap fats. Next, we used salt-assisted liquid–liquid extraction (SALLE), which uses salt to help move the chemicals into a solvent. Finally, we used dispersive liquid–liquid microextraction (DLLME), which pulls the chemicals out into a tiny drop of solvent. We then analyzed the samples with liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS), a machine that separates the chemicals and identifies each one by its weight.

We fine-tuned the method's settings using several chemometric techniques, which are statistical methods for planning experiments and finding the best settings. The smallest amounts we could detect ranged from 0.05 to 0.1 nanograms per gram of meconium (a nanogram is a billionth of a gram). When we repeated measurements on different days, the results varied by 6.5% to 14.5% of their average (this spread is called the relative standard deviation).

We checked the method in two ways. First, we made our measuring standards in meconium itself, so that the sample's own material would not throw off the readings. Then we added known amounts of the chemicals to samples and measured how much we got back. We recovered 89.9% to 114.8% of the amounts we had added.

Finally, we used the method to measure chemicals that had never been studied in meconium before, in 20 meconium samples. Our method gives information on the total exposure to these selected EDCs while the baby was still in the womb.
parts.introduction_first: Since the later part of the 20th century, industry has released a wide range of human-made chemicals, and they have reached every part of the living world, including people. Some of these chemicals can harm human health. One group is the endocrine-disrupting chemicals (EDCs), which interfere with the body's hormones. Over the past ten years, scientists have identified hundreds of chemicals as EDCs. Many studies have described the possible risks of these chemicals, both in laboratory animals and in studies of human populations. This shows how important it is to understand how EDCs affect human health and to reduce that effect.
parts.conclusion:
4. Conclusions

We successfully measured PFASs, bisphenols, parabens and benzophenones in meconium from 20 newborn babies. To prepare the samples, we used Captiva-EMR cartridges, SALLE and DLLME, and then analyzed them with LC–MS/MS. We fine-tuned the method's settings using chemometric (statistical) methods and properly checked that it worked.

To our best knowledge, this study is the first to show that PFASs are present in meconium. It also shows that other phenolic EDCs (chemicals with a particular ring-shaped structure) are present, even though they have been little studied in meconium. Our method lets us measure the total exposure to EDCs while the baby was in the womb. It also opens the way for research into whether this exposure is linked to harmful health effects.
parts.introduction_rest:
Pregnancy is one of the times when people are most easily harmed by EDCs, and some of these chemicals can change the normal way the baby develops before birth [1,2]. Exposure to EDCs while the baby is still in the womb has been linked to several problems. Newborn babies may have an unusual weight or head size [3,4]. They may have malformations of the urinary and reproductive organs [5]. Their reproductive development may be abnormal [6,7]. They may also develop problems with thinking and with how the brain and nervous system develop [8,9]. Exposure early in life has also been linked to health problems later on, including male infertility (trouble having children) [10], endometriosis (a painful condition in which tissue like the lining of the womb grows outside the womb) [11], and even cancer and the way cancer progresses [12,13,14].

So we need a good way to measure how much EDC exposure people have during pregnancy. Such measurements can help us take steps to prevent harm early and predict possible health problems in the future. Meconium has become a useful material for this. Collecting it does not hurt the baby, and it shows the total exposure to EDCs while the baby was in the womb. Meconium starts to build up in the baby's gut at around week 12 of pregnancy, and the baby passes it 24 to 72 hours after birth. Because the baby's body is not yet very active in breaking things down, meconium is thought to reflect exposure during the last two three-month periods of pregnancy, from month 4 to month 9 [15,16].

Researchers have already looked for several EDCs in meconium. These include organophosphate pesticides, pyrethroids and carbamates (three groups of insect-killing chemicals) [17,18,19], paraquat (a weedkiller) [20], polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs, long-lasting industrial chemicals) and polyaromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs, chemicals formed when things burn) [21], phthalates (chemicals used to make plastics soft) [22,23], medicines such as ibuprofen, paracetamol and atenolol, and caffeine [16]. However, we know little or nothing about whether many other substances that may harm health are present in meconium. This leaves a gap in what we know about the total exposure of babies in the womb to other foreign chemicals that are known or suspected to disrupt hormones.

In this study, we focus on four groups of EDCs that no one has yet looked for in meconium: (1) PFASs; (2) bisphenol A (BPA) and bisphenol S (BPS); (3) parabens (methyl paraben, or MPB; ethyl paraben, or EPB; propyl paraben, or PPB; and butyl paraben, or BPB); and (4) benzophenones (benzophenone 1, or BP-1; benzophenone 3, or BP-3; benzophenone-8, or BP-8; and 4-hydroxybenzophenone, or 4-OH-BP).

Each of these groups has its own uses. PFASs are widely used to coat furniture surfaces, in textiles, paper products, kitchenware and food packaging, among other things [24]. Bisphenols are the main building blocks used to make many products from epoxy resins and/or polycarbonate plastics [25]. Benzophenones are found in cosmetics, personal care products and sunscreens (where they filter out ultraviolet light), and in food packaging (where they slow down damage caused by light) [26]. Finally, parabens are cheap and kill a wide range of microbes, so they are widely used as preservatives in personal care products [27].

Meconium is a complicated mixture. From most to least common, it contains water (80%), fats, proteins, cells from the lining of the gut, fine hairs from the baby's body (called lanugo), and minerals [15]. This makes it hard to measure chemicals in it. The difficulty is especially great for human biomonitoring programs, which track the chemicals people are exposed to. These programs need methods that are accurate and sensitive, and that can be used without advanced equipment such as ultrasound machines or special devices for pulling chemicals out of samples.

So far, researchers have studied EDCs in meconium using three ways of pulling the chemicals out into a liquid: solid–liquid extraction (SLE), ultrasound-assisted extraction (UAE), and solvent pressurized liquid extraction (SPLE). They then cleaned up the samples with several steps of solid-phase extraction (SPE), which passes the liquid through a material that traps unwanted substances [16,28]. However, meconium is sticky and behaves almost like a solid, because it contains so much lanugo and gut cells. A good way to deal with this is to turn it into a liquid with an enzyme called keratinase, which breaks down the hair. Our team has used this approach before to measure selected EDCs in placenta tissue, using an enzyme called collagenase [29,30].

Once the sample is liquid, the chemicals can touch the extracting liquids much more closely. This makes it very well suited to SALLE and DLLME. Combining these two techniques has worked very well for pulling many different chemicals out of other complicated materials [31,32]. However, as far as we know, no one has yet used this approach to measure EDCs in meconium. Because meconium contains a lot of fat, it may also help to add a cleaning step before the main extraction, using special SPE devices such as Captiva EMR-Lipid cartridges. The material inside these cartridges is designed to grab the straight, unbranched chains of carbon that make up fats. This lets it recover the chemicals we want to measure very well, with precise results, in fatty materials [33,34].

Our goal was to develop and use a method to measure ten PFASs, two bisphenols, four parabens and four benzophenones in meconium. To prepare the samples, we combined Captiva-EMR cartridges with SALLE and DLLME. We then analyzed them with LC–MS/MS. We used this method on 20 meconium samples from donors who gave their samples without revealing their names. Our results show that PFASs and other phenolic EDCs (bisphenols, parabens and benzophenones) are present in meconium, even though no one had studied them in this material before.
parts.results:
3. Results and Discussion

3.1. Removing Fats with the Captiva-EMR Cartridge

We started with pooled meconium, which is meconium from many babies mixed together and melted into a liquid. We diluted small portions of it with 8 mL of acetonitrile (ACN), a solvent that is known to work well for this kind of fat removal. Earlier studies found that a mixture of 20 parts water to 80 parts ACN gives the best results in the cartridge [33,34,35].

We then dried the liquid that came out of the cartridge under a stream of nitrogen gas and dissolved it again in the same liquid we use to carry samples through the LC–MS/MS machine. The result was a cloudy solution, so it could not be injected into the machine. For this reason, we dropped the usual one-step treatment with the Captiva-EMR cartridge. Instead, we added SALLE-DLLME afterwards to remove more of the unwanted material from the meconium.

We also tried the other way round. When we used SALLE-DLLME without the cartridge first, the extracts turned into a thick, jelly-like material that the machine could not handle either. So we chose to use all three steps together: the Captiva-EMR cartridge, then SALLE, then DLLME.

3.2. Fine-Tuning the SALLE Settings

We fine-tuned three SALLE settings: the amount of table salt (sodium chloride, NaCl), the volume of formic acid added, and how long we shook the samples by hand. To do this, we used a two-level factorial design with three factors (2³). This means we tested each setting at a low and a high level, in every combination. We also added "star points", which are extra runs at levels beyond the low and high ones, and we repeated the middle setting six times. Table S1 summarizes the plan.

For each chemical, the largest signal (the largest peak area) came from a different combination of settings. To find a single best set of settings that worked well for all the chemicals at once, we used a desirability function. This is a statistical method that combines several results into one score, so we can find the best compromise when several settings affect several results at the same time [36]. The best score was 0.72 out of a perfect 1. It came with 320 mg of salt, 35.5 µL of formic acid and 60 seconds of shaking. Figure 1 shows the desirability surface, a 3D map of how the score changes as the settings change.

3.3. Fine-Tuning the DLLME Settings

Once the SALLE settings were fixed, we ran experiments to find the DLLME settings that gave the best result for each chemical. These settings were the pH of the water (how acidic it is), the percentage of salt in the water, the volume of the solvent used for extraction (TCM), and the extraction time. We used a two-level 2^(4−1) fractional factorial design, which tests half of all the possible combinations of low and high settings. We repeated the middle setting six times. Table S2 gives the range and details of this test.

Only two settings had a positive effect on PFTrA, PFHxS and BP-1: the percentage of salt in the water and the volume of TCM (Figure 2). We also checked whether our design fitted the data well, using a lack-of-fit test. This test asks whether the pattern we see is more than what the design's model would predict. For all the settings, the p-value was above 0.05. This means the test did not show a poor fit, so the design was suitable for judging whether each setting had a statistically significant effect and for finding its best value.

The best values were 10% salt in the water and 1.5 mL of TCM. We set the other settings at the most practical values: a pH of 5 for the water and an extraction time of 20 seconds.

3.4. How Well the Method Works, and Checking It

We checked four qualities of the method, following the guidelines of the US Food and Drug Administration [37]. These were linearity (whether the signal rises in a straight line as the amount of chemical rises), sensitivity (how small an amount the method can pick up), accuracy (trueness and precision), and selectivity (whether the method picks out only the chemicals we want).

To build a calibration curve for each chemical, we tested ten concentrations, four times each. A calibration curve links the machine's signal to the known amount of a chemical. We plotted the signal of each chemical divided by the signal of its mass-labeled surrogate (a specially made, slightly heavier copy of the chemical that behaves the same way) against the chemical's concentration. This gave us a range of 0.1 to 2.0 nanograms per gram for PFASs and 0.4 to 20 nanograms per gram for the phenolic compounds.

Next, we checked the matrix effect, which is how the other material in a sample changes the machine's signal. For each chemical, we made two calibration curves: one in very pure water (milliQ water, W) and one in meconium (M). We then compared their slopes, which show how steeply the signal rises with concentration. We calculated the matrix effect as a percentage like this:

ME (%) = [1 − (Slope of calibration in M/Slope of calibration in W)] × 100

For all the PFASs, the matrix effect was tiny, from −5.1% to 8.4%. For BPS, BP-1, BP-8 and 4-OH-BP, however, it was above 30%. So we needed to make our measuring standards in meconium itself. To do this, we used a pool of five blank meconium samples. We carefully chose these from a larger set of donations that were not used as analyzed samples in this study.

According to the guidelines, a sample counts as "blank" if its signal for a chemical is less than 20% of the signal at the limit of quantification (LOQ), the smallest amount we can measure reliably. Figures S1 and S2 show the machine's readouts (chromatograms) for the blank meconium pool. We added known amounts to it: 0.5 nanograms per gram for PFASs, and 10.0 nanograms per gram for bisphenols, parabens and benzophenones.

3.4.1. Accuracy (Precision and Trueness)

We added known amounts of the chemicals to pooled meconium and measured how much we got back, doing this on three days in a row. Table 2 shows the results. The spread of repeated measurements (the relative standard deviation) was below 15% in every case, which shows that the method is precise. The amounts we got back were between 89.9% and 114.8% of the amounts we had added, which shows that the method is also true.

3.4.2. Smallest Amounts We Can Detect and Measure

We defined the limit of quantification (LOQ) as the lowest concentration at which trueness and precision were within ±20%. We defined the limit of detection (LOD) as the lowest concentration at which the signal was three times greater than the background noise. Table 3 lists the LOQs and LODs for all the EDCs we studied.

3.4.3. Straight-Line Response

The signal rose in a good straight line as the amount of chemical increased. The lack-of-fit test gave p-values above 0.05, and the R² values, which show how closely the points follow the line, ranged from 99.1% to 99.6%. So we set the linear dynamic range, the range of concentrations over which the method works well, from the LOQ up to 2.0 nanograms per gram for PFASs and 20 nanograms per gram for the phenolic chemicals (Table 3).

3.4.4. Picking Out the Right Chemicals

To check selectivity, we analyzed the procedure blank, a sample that went through every step of the method but contained none of the chemicals we were looking for. We found no other chemicals showing up at the same times as our chemicals (Figure S3).

3.5. Using the Method

We used our method to measure the selected EDCs in 20 meconium samples. Every sample contained detectable amounts of various EDCs from the groups we studied, as Table 4 shows.

Of the 11 PFASs we looked for, only PFOA, PFDoA and PFTrA were found in the samples. PFOA was found in a high percentage of them. Interestingly, we did not find PFOS in any sample, even though it has often been reported in the placenta [30,38,39]. This is the first study of PFAS levels in meconium, so we cannot compare our results with other reports.

We found BPA in 50% of the samples, at concentrations ranging from undetected to 4.92 nanograms per gram. This fits with the only earlier study of BPA in meconium [40], which found BPA in 46% of samples, with a highest value of 3.93 nanograms per gram. In our study, we found BPS in only two samples (10%).

Our results for the selected parabens were similar to earlier findings in the placenta [5]. We found MPB in 100% of the meconium samples, followed by EPB (95%), PPB (65%) and BPB (40%). However, they were very different from a report by Cassoulet and colleagues [16]. They found MPB in only 20% of 396 samples from a group of people in Canada. This difference may be because their LOD for this chemical was higher (5 nanograms per gram, compared with our 0.1 nanograms per gram). Cassoulet and colleagues [16] also reported a much higher highest MPB concentration (10,415 nanograms per gram) than we did (4.91 nanograms per gram). This may reflect differences in how the people in the two studies were exposed.

Finally, we found BP-1 in 25% of the samples and BP-3 in 30%. We did not find BP-8 or 4-OH-BP in any sample. No one has studied benzophenones in meconium before, so we cannot compare our results with other reports.
parts.methods:
2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Chemicals and Other Supplies

Unless we say otherwise, all the chemicals we used were of analytical grade, which means they were very pure and suitable for careful laboratory measurements.

We bought the chemicals from Sigma-Aldrich (Madrid, Spain). These were the bisphenols bisphenol A (BPA) and bisphenol S (BPS), and a labeled version of bisphenol A called BPA-D16. We also bought the parabens methylparaben (MPB), ethylparaben (EPB), propylparaben (PPB) and butylparaben (BPB). For each of these four parabens we bought a labeled version in which the ring-shaped part of the molecule is made with a heavier form of carbon, carbon-13 (13C6). We call these MPB-13C6, EPB-13C6, PPB-13C6 and EPB-13C6. The benzophenones were benzophenone-1 (BP-1), benzophenone-3 (BP-3), benzophenone-8 (BP-8) and 4-hydroxybenzophenone (4-OH-BP), along with a labeled version of benzophenone-3 called BP-3-D5. We also bought nine PFASs: perfluorohexanoic acid (PFHxA), perfluoroheptanoic acid (PFHpA), perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA), perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA), perfluorodecanoic acid (PFDA), perfluoroundecanoic acid (PFUnA), perfluorododecanoic acid (PFDoA), perfluorotridecanoic acid (PFTrA), perfluorohexane sulfonate (PFHxS) and perfluorooctane sulfonate (PFOS).

We also used internal standards. These are versions of the chemicals that are slightly heavier, so the machine can tell them apart from the chemicals that come from the baby. They are added in known amounts to every sample, and they let us correct for small changes in the machine's readings. For the PFASs, the internal standards were 13C5-PFHxA, 13C4-PFOA, 13C2-PFDA, 13C2-PFDoA and 13C4-PFOS, supplied by Wellington Laboratories (Ontario, Canada).

We made our water very pure with a Milli-Q system (Millipore, Bedford, MA, USA). Its electrical resistance was 18.2 MΩ cm, a sign that almost nothing was dissolved in it.

We made a separate solution of each chemical we wanted to measure, and of each internal standard, at 1000 milligrams per liter (mg L−1). We dissolved them in acetonitrile, a common laboratory solvent, and kept them at 4 °C. They stayed stable for at least six months. We also made mixtures of these solutions in acetonitrile.

To fine-tune the method, to calibrate it (turn the machine's readings into amounts) and to check that it worked, we used sets of solutions with known amounts. For the PFASs these ranged from 0.005 to 0.1 mg L−1. For the bisphenols, parabens and benzophenones they ranged from 0.02 to 1.0 mg L−1. We also made solutions of 0.01 mg L−1 in acetonitrile as internal standards for the PFASs, and solutions of 0.2 mg L−1 as internal standards for the bisphenols, parabens and benzophenones.

We bought the Captiva EMR-Lipid cartridges (6 mL, 600 mg) from Agilent Technologies (Santa Clara, CA, USA). We bought HPLC-grade acetonitrile (ACN) from Merck (Darmstadt, Germany), along with LC–MS grade ACN and trichloromethane (TCM). Sigma-Aldrich (Madrid, Spain) supplied the phosphate buffer saline (PBS), a salty water solution that keeps the acidity steady, as well as sodium chloride (table salt), formic acid, ammonium acetate and an enzyme called keratinase from the bacterium Bacillus licheniformis. Keratinase breaks down keratin, the tough material in hair and skin. Just before using it, we made the enzyme solution by dissolving 0.1 mg of enzyme powder in 10 mL of PBS (0.01 M, pH 7.4).

2.2. Equipment and Software

We analyzed the samples with LC–MS/MS. The liquid chromatography part was a Shimadzu Nexera XR LC-20A system (Shimadzu, Kyoto, Japan). It was connected to an AB Sciex Triple Quadrupole (QqQ) MS/MS 5500 mass spectrometer (AB Sciex, Framingham, MA, USA). We did the statistical analyses with the program Statgraphics Centurion XVI 16.0.07 (Manugistics Inc., Rockville, MD, USA). To treat the samples with keratinase, we used a Hei-MIX incubator 1000 (Heidolph Instruments GmbH & Co, Schwabach, Germany).

2.3. Collecting and Storing the Samples

We collected meconium from 20 newborn babies at the San Cecilio Hospital in Granada, in southern Spain. All the parents gave their informed consent, meaning they agreed to donate their child's meconium after being told what the study involved. The hospital's ethics committee approved the study. Within 24 hours of birth, the nurse caring for the baby used a wooden spatula to scoop the meconium straight from the baby's first diaper. The nurse put it into a 20 mL glass container, which was then stored at −80 °C right away.

2.4. Preparing Test Samples with Known Amounts Added

We fine-tuned and checked the method using a pool of meconium from five different children. A pool is a single sample made by mixing several samples together.

To fine-tune the method, we added known amounts of the chemicals to the pooled sample. We added 0.4 nanograms per gram (ng g−1) of PFASs and 4.0 ng g−1 of bisphenols, parabens and benzophenones. To check the method, we used a wider range: 0.1 to 2.0 ng g−1 of PFASs, and 0.4 to 20.0 ng g−1 of bisphenols, parabens and benzophenones. With these we made calibration curves, which link the machine's readings to the amounts we added. We also measured how much of the added chemicals we got back.

To add the chemicals, we used a pipette to put 5 µL of the right solution (see "Chemicals and Other Supplies") into 0.2 g portions of the pooled sample. We added the internal standards in the same way, using 10 µL of the right solution. This gave 0.5 ng g−1 for the PFASs and 10 ng g−1 for the phenolic compounds (the bisphenols, parabens and benzophenones).

2.5. Turning the Samples into a Liquid with an Enzyme

In this first step, we put 0.2 g of meconium into a glass centrifuge tube and added 1.0 mL of the keratinase solution. We then kept it at 50 °C for 4 hours so that the enzyme could turn the meconium into a liquid.

2.6. Preparing the Samples for Measurement

First, we poured 8.0 mL of acetonitrile over the liquid sample. We mixed it on a vortex mixer for 60 seconds and then spun it in a centrifuge at 2600× g for 2 minutes. A centrifuge spins samples very fast so that solid bits sink to the bottom. The liquid on top is called the supernatant. We moved it into a Captiva EMR-Lipid cartridge that we had first prepared with 6 mL of a water and acetonitrile mixture (80:20 by volume). The liquid that came out of the cartridge dripped by gravity into a plastic (polypropylene) centrifuge tube. This was the sample for the SALLE-DLLME step.

For SALLE, we added 320 mg of sodium chloride (NaCl) and 35.5 µL of formic acid (98%) to the tube. We shook it by hand for 60 seconds and then spun it at 2600× g for 5 minutes. We moved the liquid on top into a 15 mL glass test tube with a screw cap. We shrank it to 1 mL under a stream of nitrogen gas and then diluted it with 10.0 mL of a 10% salt (NaCl) solution in water (by weight per volume) at pH 5.

Next, for DLLME, we injected 1.5 mL of TCM with a syringe. We shook the mixture for 20 seconds and spun it for 5 minutes at 2600× g. We moved the whole layer that had settled at the bottom into a glass vial and let it dry completely under a stream of nitrogen. Finally, we dissolved what was left in 80 µL of a mixture of water and acetonitrile (70:30 by volume). This got the sample ready to be injected into the LC–MS/MS machine.

2.7. Settings for Separating and Identifying the Chemicals

Our team has already described the settings for the chromatography and mass spectrometry in an earlier paper [30].

To separate the chemicals, we used a Gemini C18 column from Phenomenex (Torrance, CA, USA). A column is a narrow tube packed with tiny particles, and different chemicals travel through it at different speeds, so they come out at different times. Ours was 100 mm long, 2 mm wide inside, and packed with particles 3 µm across. We injected 20 μL of each sample and kept the column at 25 °C.

The liquid that carries the sample through the column is called the mobile phase. We used two liquids. Solvent A was a 5 mM solution of ammonium acetate in water (pH 6.5), and solvent B was acetonitrile. We changed the mix of the two over time, a pattern called a gradient. From 0.0 to 1.0 minutes, the mix was 30% B. From 1.0 to 5.0 minutes, B rose from 30% to 60%. From 6.0 to 8.0 minutes, it was 70% B, and from 8.0 to 8.50 minutes, it rose from 70% to 90%. From 8.50 to 9.50 minutes, it stayed at 90% B, and then it went back to 30% B in 0.1 minutes. The liquid flowed at 0.35 mL per minute, and each run took 12.0 minutes in total.

We measured the chemicals in negative ion mode, which means the machine gave the molecules a negative electric charge so it could detect them. We used selected reaction monitoring (SRM) mode, in which the machine watches for one particular molecule breaking into one particular piece. Both the first and the last stages of the machine (Q1 and Q3) could tell apart molecules that differed by just one unit of mass.

To find the best machine settings, we ran solutions of 50 µg L−1 through the machine. We set the ion source temperature to 450 ºC and the capillary voltage to −4.5 kV. Nitrogen gas served as the curtain gas at 35 psi and as ion source gases 1 and 2 at 40 psi. We adjusted all the electrical settings for each chemical, and we set the dwell time, the time the machine spends watching each signal, to 20 ms. Table 1 shows the best settings for each chemical and the signals we used to recognize it (its SRM MS/MS transitions).

2.8. Checking the Quality of Our Measurements

To check for contamination from the lab itself, we ran procedural blanks. These are samples that go through every step of the method but contain no meconium. None of them showed any measurable amount of any of the chemicals we were looking for.

We also took a pool of blank meconium samples and added known amounts of the chemicals. For the PFASs, we added 0.1, 0.2, 0.5 and 1.0 ng g−1. For the phenolic chemicals, we added 0.4, 1.0, 4.0 and 20.0 ng g−1. Every 15 injections, we injected two of these spiked blank samples.
